title: Advanced Algorithms and Complexity
text:

About the Course





This course explores advanced paradigms in algorithm design and analysis beyond the core curriculum. Students will engage with randomized and approximation algorithms, game-theoretic techniques, and the design of parallel and distributed algorithms, with applications to modern domains such as the Internet/Web and computational biology.









Prerequisites





Design and Analysis of Algorithms (CS F364) or equivalent.

Labs: Wednesday 1:00–3:00 PM (I015), Friday 1:00–3:00 PM (I015)

title: Lesson Plan: Lecture 02 — Probability Review I: Random Variables & Expectation
text:
Course: CS G526 Advanced Algorithms & Complexity Duration: 50 Minutes Topic: Random Variables, Expectation, and Linearity of Expectation Objectives: 1. Recall core probability concepts (sample spaces, events, axioms). 2. Define discrete and continuous random variables and mathematical expectation. 3. Understand and apply Linearity of Expectation (specifically for non-independent variables using Indicator RVs).



gantt
    title Lecture 02 Agenda (50 Mins)
    dateFormat HH:mm
    axisFormat %M
    section Introduction
    Recap and Motivation :active, 00:00, 00:05
    section Probability Basics
    Sample Spaces and Axioms : 00:05, 00:15
    Random Variables and Expectation: 00:15, 00:30
    section Core Tool
    Linearity and Indicators : 00:30, 00:45
    section Wrap-Up
    Concept Check and Wrap-Up : 00:45, 00:50









Time
Duration
Activity / Content
Pedagogical Goal / Board Work




00:00–00:05
5 mins
Recap & Motivation: Quick recap of the four paradigms. Discuss why probability is the core language of randomized algorithms (analyzing average-case inputs vs. introducing random coin flips in execution).
Set the stage for why a rigorous review is necessary.


00:05–00:15
10 mins
Sample Space, Events, Axioms: Briefly define sample space \Omega, events \mathcal{F}, probability measure \Pr, and Kolmogorov’s axioms.
Board Work: Write down axioms. Keep it brief to focus on calculations.


00:15–00:30
15 mins
Random Variables & Expectation: Define Random Variables (RVs) and Expectation E[X] = \sum x \Pr[X=x]. Walk through expected value of a single fair coin flip or die roll.
Mathematical Focus: Clearly define discrete expectation and its properties.


00:30–00:45
15 mins
Linearity of Expectation: Introduce E[\sum X_i] = \sum E[X_i]. Emphasize that no independence is required. Introduce Indicator Random Variables (I_A = 1 if A occurs, 0 otherwise) and the fundamental identity E[I_A] = \Pr[A]. Walk through the expected number of fixed points in a random permutation.
Active Derivation: Derive the expectation of fixed points using indicators on the board. Show how independence doesn’t matter.


00:45–00:50
5 mins
Concept Check & Next Class Preview: Run the concept check question. Preview Lecture 3 (Variance, Moments, and Complexity Classes).
Check students’ understanding of indicator RVs.










Expectation definition (discrete): E[X] = \sum_{x} x \cdot \Pr[X = x]
Linearity of Expectation Theorem: For any random variables X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n (independent or not): E\left[\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right] = \sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i]





For an event A, let: X_A = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } A \text{ occurs} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
Fundamental Lemma: E[X_A] = 1 \cdot \Pr[A] + 0 \cdot \Pr[\bar{A}] = \Pr[A]





Let \pi be a random permutation of \{1, 2, \dots, n\}. What is the expected number of fixed points (elements i such that \pi(i) = i)?
Let X be the number of fixed points. Let X_i be the indicator that \pi(i) = i.
X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
E[X_i] = \Pr[\pi(i) = i] = \frac{1}{n}
By linearity: E[X] = E\left[\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right] = \sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i] = n \cdot \frac{1}{n} = 1
Key takeaway: The expected number of fixed points is exactly 1, regardless of n. Note that X_i and X_j are highly dependent, yet linearity holds!







Expectation with Balls & Bins: > Question: “Suppose we throw n balls independently and uniformly at random into n bins. What is the expected number of empty bins?” > Answer: > - Let X be the number of empty bins. Let X_i be the indicator that bin i is empty. > - A bin i is empty if all n balls miss it. The probability that a single ball misses bin i is 1 - 1/n. > - Since the balls are thrown independently, the probability that all n balls miss bin i is: > \Pr[\text{bin } i \text{ is empty}] = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^n > - By linearity: > E[X] = \sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i] = n \cdot \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^n > - As n \to \infty, this approaches: > n \cdot e^{-1} \approx 0.368 n > - Pedagogical Tip: Highlight that about 36.8% of the bins are expected to remain empty.

title: Lesson Plan: Lecture 01 — Course Overview & the Landscape of Advanced Algorithms
text:
Course: CS G526 Advanced Algorithms & Complexity Duration: 50 Minutes Topic: Introduction to Advanced Algorithmic Paradigms Objectives: 1. Situate the course in the overall algorithmic toolkit (beyond core Data Structures and Algorithms). 2. Define and contrast the four core paradigms: Randomized, Approximation, Game-theoretic/Online, and Parallel/Distributed. 3. Understand the syllabus roadmap, evaluation components, and course logistics.



gantt
    title Lecture 01 Agenda (50 Mins)
    dateFormat  HH:mm
    axisFormat %M
    section Introduction
    Welcome and Course Logistics   :active, 00:00, 00:15
    section Core Concepts
    Defining "Advanced" Paradigms: 00:15, 00:35
    Applications and Motivation    : 00:35, 00:45
    section Wrap-Up
    Concept Check and Next Class   : 00:45, 00:50









Time
Duration
Activity / Content
Pedagogical Goal / Board Work




00:00–00:15
15 mins
Welcome & Course Logistics: Introduce course info, evaluation scheme, textbooks (T1, T2, reference books), consultation hours, and lab timings.
Establish expectations. Highlight the 20% weight on the Term Project (Proposal + Presentation + Report).


00:15–00:35
20 mins
What is “Advanced”? The Four Paradigms: Discuss why standard polynomial-time exact sequential algorithms are insufficient. Introduce: (1) Randomized (trading certainty for efficiency); (2) Approximation (trading optimality for runtime); (3) Game-theoretic/Online (handling incomplete info); (4) Parallel & Distributed (scaling via hardware).
Board Work: Write down the 4 paradigms with a one-sentence summary of what they trade off (e.g. certainty, optimality, space/time, etc.).


00:35–00:45
10 mins
Application Domains: Illustrate paradigms using real-world domains like PageRank/Rec Systems (Online/Randomized) and Sequence Alignment/BLAST (Approximation/Parallel).
Real-world context: Show how modern services (Google search, Amazon recommendations) are built on these paradigms rather than standard sorting/searching.


00:45–00:50
5 mins
Concept Check & Next Class Preview: Run a brief concept check to test intuition on the 4 paradigms. Preview Lecture 2 (Probability Review).
Active learning. Gauge student readiness for mathematical review.










Write this table on the board to illustrate what each paradigm trades off:










Paradigm
Input/Environment
What We Optimize
What We Trade Off / Accept




Randomized
Fixed / Arbitrary
Expected Runtime / Error Rate
Small chance of failure or varying runtime


Approximation
Fixed / NP-Hard
Approximate Solution Quality
Exact global optimality (accept \alpha-optimal)


Online / Game-theoretic
Arrives Sequentially / Strategic
Competitive Ratio / Regret
Full knowledge of future inputs


Parallel / Distributed
Shared or Partitioned
Work and Depth (Speedup)
Single-core synchronous model







Draw a rough timeline on the board:

Weeks 1–3: Foundations & Concentration Bounds (Module 1, 2)
Weeks 4–5: Randomized Structures & Graph Algorithms (Module 3)
Weeks 6–7: Games & Online Decisions (Module 4, 5)
Week 8: Algebraic & Number-Theoretic Algorithms (Module 6)
Week 9: Parallel & Distributed Systems (Module 7)
Week 10: Advanced Counting / Tutte Matrix (Module 8)
Weeks 11–12: Approximation & Inapproximability (Module 9)
Week 13: Web & Biological Networks (Module 10)
Week 14: Project Presentations (Module 11)








Paradigms and Uncertainty: > Question: “Which algorithmic paradigm specifically handles uncertainty in: (a) Inputs arriving dynamically over time? (b) Algorithm runtime? (c) Solution quality for NP-hard problems?” > Answer: > - (a) Online / Game-theoretic Algorithms (decisions must be made without knowing the future). > - (b) Randomized Algorithms (specifically Las Vegas algorithms where runtime is a random variable, but the answer is always correct). > - (c) Approximation Algorithms (we guarantee a solution within a factor \alpha of the optimal).
The Project Proposal Requirement: > Question: “What constitutes a good Term Project topic for this course?” > Answer: An ideal project involves either applying one of the four paradigms to a domain of interest (e.g., bio-informatics, web graphs, parallel systems) or implementing and evaluating/extending a modern algorithm from recent literature.
